Q: Couldn't install Microsoft.VisualStudio.Community.Shared.Msi A:

Whoever faced such an issue and desperately tried every possible solutions like me: I found another extra solution for that and it helped me.

First I found C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\VisualStudio\Packages\Microsoft.VisualStudio.Community.Shared.Msi,version=18.4.11506.43\ that actual msi component app. Then just run it, if you don't have any issue, it will work without error messages. But you are already here then you have a problem with that. That app show you what exact Registry Editor key missing or not working. Just copy that key name.

Then according to Registry Editor, it is not working when you try to open \Components folder from that path HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Installer\UserData\S-1-5-18\Components\. You can create or change any Key from PowerShell as admin with some commands.
That's the creating missing key commands step by step:

  1. New-Item -Path "HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Installer\UserData\S-1-5-18\Components\90C68BBCA565FC341902D954EA3347AC" -Force
  2. $key = "HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Installer\UserData\S-1-5-18\Components\90C68BBCA565FC341902D954EA3347AC"
  3. $acl = Get-Acl $key
  4. $rule = New-Object System.Security.AccessControl.RegistryAccessRule("SYSTEM","FullControl","ContainerInherit,ObjectInherit","None","Allow")
  5. $acl.SetAccessRule($rule)
  6. Set-Acl -Path $key -AclObject $acl

After that, just Restart you pc. Retry your Visual Studio installer.

Q: How to convert a python datetime.timedelta to years? A:

Different years can differ in length. 365 days is only a year if it's not in a leap year.

A datetime.timedelta on its own only specifies an abstract number of days. Turning two dates into a delta removes critical information about which dates are in question.

So you need to work on the specific dates in question.

from datetime import date


def years(start: date, end: date) -> int:
    """Return whole years between dates dropping fractional years."""
    if end < start:
        start, end = end, start
    if start.month == 2 and start.day == 29:  # noqa: PLR2004
        start = start.replace(day=28)
    return end.year - start.year - ((end.month, end.day) < (start.month, start.day))


tests = (
    ("2024-04-19", "2024-04-20", 0),
    ("2024-04-20", "2024-04-19", 0),
    ("2024-04-20", "2024-04-20", 0),
    ("2024-04-20", "2024-04-30", 0),
    ("2024-04-30", "2024-04-20", 0),
    ("2024-01-01", "2024-12-31", 0),
    ("2024-01-01", "2025-01-01", 1),
    ("2024-01-01", "2025-12-31", 1),
    ("2024-02-28", "2025-02-28", 1),
    ("2024-02-29", "2025-02-27", 0),
    ("2024-02-29", "2025-02-28", 1),
    ("2024-02-29", "2025-03-01", 1),
    ("2023-02-27", "2024-02-29", 1),
    ("2023-02-28", "2024-02-29", 1),
)

tests = list((date.fromisoformat(a), date.fromisoformat(b), c) for (a, b, c) in tests)
assert all(years(start, end) == result for (start, end, result) in tests)

Q: Redis Sentinel vs clustering A:

First, let’s talk Sentinel.

Sentinel manages the failover; it doesn't configure Redis for HA. It is an important distinction. Second, the diagram you posted is actually a bad setup. You don't want to run Sentinel on the same node as the Redis nodes it is managing. When you lose that host you lose both.

As to "Is it waste of resources?" it depends on your use case. You don't need three Redis nodes in that setup; you only need two. Three increases your redundancy, but it is not required. If you need the added redundancy, then it isn't a waste of resources. If you don't need redundancy, then you just run a single Redis instance and call it good, as running more would be "wasted".

Another reason for running two slaves would be to split reads. Again, if you need it then it wouldn't be a waste.

As to "Is there a better way of using full use of the resources available?" we can't answer that as it is far too dependent on your specific scenario and code. That said, if the amount of data to store is "small" and the command rate is not exceedingly high, then remember you don't need to dedicate a host to Redis.

Now for "Is Redis clustering an alternative to Redis sentinel?". It really depends entirely on your use case. Redis Cluster is not an HA solution. It is a multiple writer/larger-than-ram solution. If your goal is just HA, then it likely won't be suitable for you. Redis Cluster comes with limitations, particularly around multi-key operations, so it isn't necessarily a straightforward "just use cluster" operation.

If you think having three hosts running Redis (and three running sentinel) is wasteful, you'll likely hold Cluster to be even more so, as it does require more resources.

The questions you've asked are probably too broad and opinion-based to survive as written. If you have a specific case/problem you are working out, please update with that so we can provide specific assistance and information.

For the specifics:

For proper failover management in your scenario, I would go with three sentinels, one running on your JBoss server. If you have three JBoss nodes, then go with one on each. I'd have a Redis pod (master+slave) on separate nodes, and let Sentinel manage the failover.

From there it is a matter of wiring up JBoss/Jedis to use Sentinel for its information and connection management. As I don't use those, a quick search turns up that Jedis has the support for it. You just need to configure it correctly. Some examples I found are at How can I set up a connection to Redis Sentinel using Jedis library? and How can I use the Jedis API to handle failover (i.e., when the master server goes down)? #725 which talk about JedisSentinelPool being the route for using a pool.

When Sentinel executes a failover the clients will be disconnected and Jedis will (should?) handle the reconnection by asking the Sentinels who the current master is.

Q: Do I need Jedis to use Redis cache in Spring Boot? A:

By adding spring-boot-starter-data-redis dependency and adding spring annotation like @Cacheble @CacheEvict the redis caching will work fine. But to leverage advanced features like clustering ,pipelining, asynchronous operation,thread safety and high performance you can consider using jedis for implementation
